title: Smooth connected groups of multiplicative type are tori
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme]. An $S$-group scheme has multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying the group diagrams; a homomorphism respects them. A group of multiplicative type of finite presentation is an fppf-local form of $D(M)=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_S[M]$ for a finitely generated abelian group $M$, with $e_m\mapsto e_m\otimes e_m$ as comultiplication [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group]. Fppf means faithfully flat and locally of finite presentation [def-pc-fppf-site]. A torus is an fppf-local form of $\mathbf G_m^r$ for a finite integer $r\geq0$, where $\mathbf G_m(U)=\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)^\times$. Let $P\to S$ be a group of multiplicative type of finite presentation. If $P\to S$ is smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] and every geometric fibre of $P\to S$ is connected [def-weil-connected-scheme], then $P$ is a torus. More explicitly, there is an fppf covering of $S$ on which $P$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^{r_i}$ for finite ranks $r_i$. This permits disconnected or nonreduced bases and requires geometric connectedness of the whole fibre, not merely of its identity component.

source.place: Appendix B, Proposition B.3.4 and its character-sheaf description of tori; smooth connected diagonalizable fibres have torsion-free character groups. This is the relative torus-recognition criterion, not a definition of tori. WANTED locally as literature/conrad-reductive-group-schemes.pdf.

proof.text: By the multiplicative-type hypothesis choose an fppf covering $\{U_i\to S\}$ and group isomorphisms $P_{U_i}\simeq D_{U_i}(M_i)$ with each $M_i$ finitely generated; the covering convention is [def-pc-fppf-site]. Discard empty members. Fix one remaining $U=U_i$ and write $M=M_i$. Choose a point $u\in U$, an affine open $V=\operatorname{Spec}R$ containing it, and an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of $\kappa(u)$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure, def-weil-geometric-point]. The composite $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to U\to S$ is a geometric point of $S$. On $V$, the splitting has coordinate algebra $R[M]$ [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group]. The affine fibre-product formula and tensor universal property identify its pullback with $\operatorname{Spec}\Omega[M]$: the inverse algebra maps are $a\otimes\sum_m r_me_m\mapsto\sum_m a\bar r_me_m$ and $\sum_m a_me_m\mapsto\sum_m a_m\otimes e_m$. Their composites fix the displayed generators. Thus the geometric fibre of $P$ at this composite is $D_\Omega(M)$, not a different fibre of a quotient or of an identity component.

source.place: Examples 12.1--12.2 and Remark 12.6, printed pp.231--232; explicit extension-of-scalars calculation over R. Stacks 01I4, schemes-lemma-fibre-product-affine-schemes.

proof.text: Smoothness of $P\to S$ gives geometrically reduced fibres by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced]. Therefore $D_\Omega(M)$ is reduced, and $A=\Omega[M]$ has no nonzero nilpotents by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-scheme-reduced-iff]. It is connected because every geometric fibre of $P\to S$ is assumed connected. Suppose $\operatorname{char}\Omega=p>0$ and $M$ has an element $m$ of finite order $n>1$ divisible by $p$. Then $a=(n/p)m$ has order $p$. In the basis of [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group], $z=e_a-e_0$ is nonzero, whereas the characteristic-$p$ binomial identity gives $z^p=e_{pa}-e_0=0$, a contradiction. Consequently no finite-order element of $M$ has order divisible by the residue characteristic. This step is applied to the original smooth morphism $P\to S$; it assumes no reducedness of $S$ or of the splitting cover.

source.place: Tag 056T, lemma-smooth-geometrically-normal, with morphisms.tex Tag 01VB, lemma-base-change-smooth; schemes.tex Tag 01J2, lemma-affine-reduced. The nilpotent calculation expands Milne Remark 12.5, p.232.

proof.text:
If $m\in M$ has order $n>1$, Step 2 ensures that $n$ is invertible in $\Omega$ (also automatic in characteristic zero). Set $b=n^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}e_{jm}\in A$. Each residue class modulo $n$ occurs exactly $n$ times among the sums of two such indices, so $b^2=n^{-2}n\sum_j e_{jm}=b$. The $n$ basis elements are distinct. The coefficient of $e_m$ is $n^{-1}
e0$, proving both $b
e0$ and $b
e1$. By [lem-weil-pbc-spec-clopen-idempotent], $D(b)$ and $D(1-b)$ are complementary clopens. Neither is empty: under its bijection, the empty set corresponds to $0$ and the whole spectrum to $1$. This contradicts connectedness [def-weil-connected-scheme]. Thus $M$ is torsion-free. These are explicit basis and idempotent calculations, not an appeal to a torus-recognition theorem.

source.place: Tag 00EE, lemma-disjoint-decomposition; elementary averaging-idempotent calculation expanding Milne Remark 12.5, printed p.232.

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-fg-torsionfree-group-free] to this finitely generated torsion-free $M$. Choose its finite basis $b_1,\ldots,b_r$. On every affine open $\operatorname{Spec}B\subset U$, the inverse algebra maps $B[M]\rightleftarrows B[x_1^{\pm1},\ldots,x_r^{\pm1}]$ send $e_{\sum_j n_jb_j}\mapsto\prod_jx_j^{n_j}$ and $\prod_jx_j^{n_j}\mapsto e_{\sum_j n_jb_j}$. Unique expression in the basis makes them well defined; addition of exponents proves multiplicativity. They preserve coproduct, counit and antipode on each basis monomial [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group]. The affine-spectrum construction therefore makes them inverse group-scheme maps [def-weil-affine-spectrum]; the tensor-product and affine-product formulas identify the Laurent spectrum with $\mathbf G_{m,B}^{r}$. Here, for every $B$-scheme $T$, the Spec--global-sections bijection [lem-a1-locally-ringed-space-affine-adjunction] identifies $B$-morphisms $T\to\operatorname{Spec}B[x^{\pm1}]$ with $B$-algebra maps $B[x^{\pm1}]\to\Gamma(T,\mathcal O_T)$, i.e. with units $\Gamma(T,\mathcal O_T)^\times$ (image of $x$), naturally in $T$, and the coproduct $x\mapsto x\otimes x$ with multiplication of units; so $\operatorname{Spec}B[x^{\pm1}]$ represents $\mathbf G_{m,B}$ as a group functor. These formulas fix coefficients and commute with restriction, so define inverse maps of the corresponding algebra sheaves on $U$, giving $D_U(M)\simeq\mathbf G_{m,U}^{r}$. Composing with the given splitting gives $P_U\simeq\mathbf G_{m,U}^{r}$. Perform this construction for every nonempty covering member. The original fppf cover thus proves exactly the stated torus property, with ranks allowed to vary. Rank zero uses $B[0]=B$ and the empty product; if $S$ is empty the empty covering suffices.
